Eriadorians — Rural

Rural upbringing: animals, fieldcraft, survival and practical skills.

Eriadorians are the Common Men of the lands once ruled by Arnor: Arthedain, Cardolan, Rhudaur, and neighbouring districts. Their communities have different customs, but share memories of the Northern Kingdom, the use of Westron, and centuries of contact with the Dúnedain.

Origins and lineages

Their ancestry draws in varying degrees upon the ancient Men of the West, Daen peoples, Northmen, and descendants of Númenor. Some families recall the Dúnedain in stature, features, or longevity; others resemble the ordinary inhabitants of Eriador's towns and countryside. This Culture represents those who make their lives in Eriador without belonging to its great Dúnadan houses.

Appearance

The same diversity is apparent in their build: slender or sturdy, Eriadorians are usually of average height. Men commonly stand around five feet ten inches and women around five feet four inches.

Their complexions may be fair, tanned, or slightly olive. Every hair and eye color occurs among them, reflecting the many peoples who mingled in ancient Arnor. Their life expectancy is comparable to that of other Common Men, generally between sixty and eighty years. Certain families marked by Dúnedain ancestry may nevertheless live noticeably longer.

Territories and communities

Eriador is a broad land whose communities lead very different lives. Some still occupy the old market towns or trade roads of the Northern Kingdom; others dwell in isolated villages, remote valleys, farming estates, or grazing lands far from any centre of authority.

Urban life

In market towns, river ports, and trading crossroads, Eriadorians work as craftspeople, merchants, guards, innkeepers, boatmen, labourers, and scribes. Guilds and markets bring them into contact with travellers, Dúnedain, Dwarves, Hobbits, and many others living in the region.

Rural life

In the countryside, farming, herding, forestry, fishing, and hunting provide most livelihoods. Fieldwork, fairs, the seasons, and family obligations shape the year. Many know their valley and neighbouring villages far better than the former capitals of Arnor.

Temperament and hospitality

Practical and usually faithful to their commitments, Eriadorians value straightforward agreements and useful work. Generations of danger amid the ruins of the North—Orcs, brigands, wild beasts, and war—have taught their communities caution.

Their reserve often conceals remarkable persistence. A farmer or craftsperson may care above all for home, kin, and land, yet that everyday loyalty can inspire unexpected courage when a village or neighbourhood is threatened.

Town dwellers, accustomed to strangers passing through, are generally more at ease in negotiation. Rural families tend to be more cautious with newcomers, particularly armed travellers, wizards, or emissaries from distant lands.

Towns, villages, and architecture

Arnor's buildings still shape many towns: stone walls, paved roads, bridges, towers, and halls stand among more recent houses. Eriadorians may have used these works for generations without knowing exactly who built them.

Rural settlements are more modest. Timber or stone farmhouses, barns, sheepfolds, mills, and small inns form hamlets sometimes enclosed by a palisade. Tools and weapons of wood, leather, bronze, or iron are built for durability, while wool and linen provide most clothing.

Clothing

Eriadorians wear practical wool and linen clothing suited to Eriador's sometimes damp and cold climate. In milder regions, men wear knee-length tunics held by broad belts, while women may wear a short tunic over a long linen skirt.

In cooler regions, clothing generally includes a linen shirt, woolen tunic, breeches or a heavy skirt, hose, sturdy boots, and a long hooded cloak. Linen cloth often remains white or undyed, while wool is colored in subdued green, grey, brown, or other shades easy to produce locally.

Family

Marriage is generally monogamous. Depending on local custom, descent may be traced through the father or the mother, reflecting the varied peoples who mingled within the old Northern Kingdom.

Family ties shape Eriadorian communities. In the countryside, several generations may share a farm or occupy neighbouring holdings, passing land, livestock, tools, and duties among kin. In towns, guilds, fraternities, and neighbourhood loyalties add bonds based on work to those of family.

Beliefs and local customs

Beliefs differ from one district to another and are generally practised quietly. Most honour Eru and the Valar through family and local customs, without a powerful priesthood or large religious institutions.

Alongside reverence for Eru and the Valar, many local customs endure. Springs, ancient trees, hills, standing stones, and ruins are associated with stories and sometimes taboos. A community may honour a forgotten hero, respect a protective spring, or avoid a supposedly haunted grove without regarding these practices as a separate religion.

Araw, their name for Oromë, is regarded by many Eriadorians as the protector of hunters, travellers, and Common Men. In rural districts, Yavanna—sometimes called Dalam or Aedalam—is especially honoured for the fertility of the land, the harvest, and the growth of plants.

Languages

Westron predominates, with regional accents that can immediately reveal a traveller's origins. Near old Dúnadan settlements, some also learn Sindarin or Adûnaic; elsewhere neighbouring tongues and forms of Dunael supplement local speech.

Relations with neighbouring peoples

People in Eriador's towns and market settlements are familiar with dealings beyond their own communities. They trade with Dwarves, welcome Hobbits, negotiate with neighbours, and may acknowledge Dúnadan authority when local customs or interests call for it.

Rural suspicion chiefly reflects isolation and fear of unrest. Strangers with unfamiliar habits are received cautiously. Orcs and Wargs, by contrast, meet almost universal hostility, sustained by memories of the raids and wars that devastated Eriador.

Old Dúnedain ancestry

Many families tell of a Dúnadan forebear. For some, that ancestry belongs chiefly to the stories handed down at home; in others, it is evident in longer lives, stronger resistance to illness, or greater-than-average stature.

Such an inheritance may come from a noble who settled far from court, an obscure younger branch, an old marriage with an Arthedain or Cardolan family, or a community that retained some Númenórean ancestry.

Occupations and training

Eriadorian communities place considerable value on practical skills useful in daily life and travel. Their people include fighters, rogues, thieves, craftsmen, hunters, scouts, soldiers, healers, innkeepers, merchants, sailors, and travellers.

Magic is uncommon and often met with caution or fear. Animists and a few semi-spell-users may live among them, but pure or hybrid magical traditions remain exceptional. The Barbarian profession is likewise poorly suited to this Culture's usual way of life.

In towns, training commonly involves trade, diplomacy, specialised crafts, administration, navigation, the arts, languages, and guild occupations. Rural communities place greater emphasis on survival, tracking, animal husbandry, hunting, foraging, leatherworking, woodworking, weather lore, and travel over difficult ground.

Weapons

Eriadorians mainly use simple weapons that are easy to maintain: dagger, hatchet, club, throwing dagger, sling, staff, and fishing spear. Militia, town guards, and soldiers may use swords, spears, bows, shields, and heavier armor.

Eriadorian characters

This Culture suits a character from the Angle, Bree-land, Cardolan, Arthedain, or Rhudaur, as well as the people of the valleys, market towns, villages, and farming estates of the old Northern Kingdoms.

Eriadorians live among roads, ruins, and old place-names that still recall Arnor. Their own history, however, is not simply that of its high Númenórean nobility. They maintain farms and workshops, travel to markets, and defend their homes despite the wars and dangers of the North.
